top.line: Founders are developers who do not call it that
top.para: Every GenAI founder Dinis knows does a development team's jobs and denies being a developer, because they never saw how rough new technology is inside. Since a book addressed to a word its readers reject loses them, his hypothesis is to call it Generation ZX Founders, with the reveal at the end.

in-short.line: Developers in all but name; rename the book
in-short.para: Founders do the roles of a whole team, often no worse than the industry. They only saw polished products, and now meet the non-functional requirements. Programming was never just code. So the book may be Generation ZX Founders.

look.line: They laugh when told they are developers
look.para: Friends building companies deny being developers: they just tell the model what to do. Yet they write requirements, test, release and direct a team of agents, mostly in the explorer phase, some assembling commodity components.

crude.line: Crude, but the industry often does worse
crude.para: Many companies underinvest, outsource, underfund teams and ship anyway, which is why vulnerabilities are everywhere, even in big companies' internal tools. A vulnerability is an engineering gap; internal tools never had the market's beating, which is where the SaaS apocalypse may land first.

sausage.line: They never saw how new products really work
sausage.para: Founders know polished, later-generation products. The iPhone was launched on a golden path of taps with signal bars hard-coded; Windows 98 crashed on stage beside Gates; Apple's interfaces began as Director mock-ups. The demo gods are explorer technology hanging by a thread.

relieved.line: The demo team's relief worries the customer
relieved.para: When a demo works, the presenters are visibly relieved, and the customer wonders whether it was supposed to fail, like a pilot celebrating a safe landing.

unfinished.line: Unfinished work made to look unfinished
unfinished.para: Developers gave mock-ups rough, hand-drawn themes so the business would not ship them, as Bootswatch's Sketchy and Napkin Look and Feel do, following Joel Spolsky's 2002 point that a beautiful screen looks almost done to a non-programmer.

understand.line: Now they meet the non-functional requirements
understand.para: Building for themselves, business people now complain about versioning, breakage, design alignment, stability and security, the requirements that were never funded. Seeing inside a technology company would show them how good they already are.

programming.line: Programming is not just writing code
programming.para: People who say they do not program build serious things in Excel and professional tools. That is programming; code is a small part of development, and the citizen developer is good news.

book.para: Calling readers developers loses the people the book is for. Founder is a word they recognise and a better-qualified audience. The argument that they are developers, now chapter 8, would move to the end as a reveal, under decision 014's process.

limits.para: Every founder Dinis knows is his experience. The title is a hypothesis; decision 014 stands. The iPhone story is one reporter's account; Apple's Director prototypes were internal. Being a developer does not mean the work is ready.

sources.line: A memo and the primary sources
sources.para: Dinis's memo of 19 October 2026, Vogelstein's NYT Magazine piece, the 1998 AP report, James Thomson on the Dock, Joel Spolsky, Bootswatch and Napkin, and the book's decisions.
